title: Ai Adoption: Practice Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: In the worked example, Priya's network keeps adoption numbers climbing even after she is reassigned to another project for six weeks. What best explains that outcome?
options: The AI tool became so reliable that nobody needed support
Priya's north-star metric was set too low to matter
The champions were tied to the way of working rather than to the launch, and had the time, structure, and recognition to keep playing their rhythm without her
The company stopped requiring coordinators to use the tool
questions.explanation: Priya selected champions by influence and bandwidth, gave them a monthly circle, a defined support role, and an ongoing post-launch job. Because the support role belonged to the champions, not to Priya, the network carried adoption when she was pulled away. This reflects the lesson's core point that the support role outlives any single owner.

questions.question: An adoption owner is picking champions for a company AI rollout and is tempted to choose the three loudest volunteers. Based on the lesson, what is the most important correction to that approach?
options: Choose people primarily by their technical skill with the tool
Choose people with existing influence in each department and check bandwidth, because influence and available time are what actually move adoption
Pick only people from departments that already support the AI rollout
Pick as many volunteers as possible so no department is left out, regardless of their role
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that the loudest volunteer is not always the most influential person, and influence is the trait that moves adoption. It also stresses representation across the whole organization and checking bandwidth so champions have time to help. Selecting for influence and time, not enthusiasm or technical skill alone, makes the network work.

questions.question: In the four-track adoption audit, which track is the one that captures the data flowing into AI tools, such as the recruiting coordinator pasting candidate resumes into a free consumer tool?
options: The tool track, which lists every AI tool in use
The workflow track, which maps which jobs and steps use AI
The perception track, which compares leader estimates to worker reports
The data track, which records what information is entered or uploaded into the tools
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the data track as recording what kinds of information are typed, pasted, or uploaded into these tools, the risk surface that a future data policy and incident response will need to account for. The candidate-resume example is presented as a data-track finding.

questions.question: Lesson 2 gives five tests for whether a workflow is ready for AI. Which profile best describes work where AI is most likely to create value?
options: High volume, predictable inputs, a clear checkable output, cheap errors, and repeatable steps
Rare, high-stakes judgment calls where a wrong answer is hard to detect and expensive to fix
Open-ended creative work that is the organization's differentiator and has no objective ground truth
Any work where people are enthusiastic about the tool, regardless of volume or structure
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 defines value-ready work as having structured, repeatable inputs; a clear output someone consumes; an output that can be checked cheaply; errors that are cheap to fix; and enough volume that gains accumulate. Rare, high-stakes judgment calls and open-ended creative work fail several of those tests.

questions.question: After a pilot team posts a strong first-month win, which step does the lesson warn leaders most often skip, and why does it matter?
options: Creating short-term wins, because without a visible win no one will believe the change works
Consolidating gains and producing more change, because declaring victory too early lets the old ways reassert themselves before the change is anchored
Building a guiding coalition, because the pilot team alone cannot sustain the change
Communicating the vision, because people forget why the change matters
questions.explanation: The lesson flags Kotter's seventh step, consolidate gains and produce more change, as the one most leaders skip. Declaring victory too early is a serious error because the change is not yet anchored, so the correct move after a win is to use its credibility to push into the next workflow.

questions.question: Lesson 1 defines the relationship between a rollout and a running program. Which describes it correctly?
options: A rollout is the ongoing work of sustaining adoption, while a program is the one-time launch effort
A rollout is a bounded effort with a timeline and an end, while a running program is ongoing work with no finish line
A rollout and a running program are the same thing under different names
A running program is a single training session, while a rollout manages usage over time
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 defines rollout as a bounded effort with a goal, steps, timeline, and end, and a running program as the ongoing work of sustaining adoption, measuring value, and governing use, with no finish line. AI adoption is a program, not a project.

questions.question: A manager funded a two-week launch campaign and usage climbed during it. When the campaign ended, usage collapsed. What does this pattern most directly indicate?
options: The usage was driven by the launch event, so it was a spike rather than compounding momentum
The adoption is momentum and will resume on its own
The tool only works during high-energy campaigns
The users need more training before they can adopt the tool
questions.explanation: The lesson's test separates the two: a spike depends on the thing that started it and collapses when the event stops, while momentum runs on its own returns. If usage collapses when the launch event ends, what you had was a spike, not momentum.

questions.question: In Lesson 1's worked example, what single root failure do Dana's shadow IT, usage decay, and client-data incident all share?
options: She chose the wrong vendor for the rollout
She ran the rollout and stopped, never starting the ongoing program it required
She spent too much budget on licenses
She made the IT team the adoption owner
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 reads all three failures as the same failure wearing different clothes: Dana ran a rollout and stopped. The shadow IT was a governance gap, the decay was a momentum gap, and the incident was a risk gap, all of which a running program with a policy, review cadence, and owner would have contained.

questions.question: According to the McKinsey survey cited in Lesson 1, which finding most directly supports the case that an adoption owner's job is a program, not a rollout?
options: 70 percent of employees personally feel ready for AI while only 27 percent of leaders believe their organizations are ready to change around it
Employees are less ready for AI than their organizations are
Individual readiness accounts for 48 percent of value capture, nearly twice the share of organizational readiness
Treating AI as a technology deployment reliably captures the most enterprise value
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 cites McKinsey's survey: 70 percent of employees feel personally ready while only 27 percent of leaders believe their organizations are ready, and organizational readiness (48 percent) matters nearly twice as much as personal readiness (25 percent). This shows the value comes from ongoing organizational change, which is the program.

questions.question: A leader plans to treat the first 30 days of an AI rollout as the entire change effort. What does the habit-formation research cited in the lesson say about that plan?
options: A 30-day window is sufficient because workplace change is more structured than a daily personal habit
A habit reliably forms in 21 days for most people, so 30 days is generous
The median time to automaticity was 66 days with a range of 18 to 254 days, and even that describes a selected group, so a month is too short
Most participants in the study formed habits within 30 days, so the plan is reasonable
questions.explanation: The lesson grounds the '30-day on-ramp is too short' thesis in the Lally study: a median of 66 days to reach the modeled automaticity plateau, a range of 18 to 254 days, and even that figure describes a selected subset of motivated volunteers. A month is the beginning of the change effort, not the end.

questions.question: A company's AI project team completes the rollout and disbands, ending the formal change-agent role. Why does the lesson say the support network should keep operating after this point?
options: To replace the vendor's customer support entirely
Because a super user belongs to the system, not the project, and carries adoption for as long as the way of working is in use, which prevents value leaking out after implementation
Because the network is required to train new leaders only
To reduce the number of support tickets the IT team handles for unrelated software
questions.explanation: The lesson draws the distinction that a change agent belongs to the project and ends at go-live, while a super user belongs to the system and lasts for as long as it is used. It cites McKinsey's finding that 20 percent of transformation value is lost after implementation, which is exactly the window an ongoing peer support network operates in.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why is it not enough to run only a voluntary survey asking people to self-report their AI use?
options: Surveys are always invalid and should never be used in an audit
Self-report is the most reliable single source and needs no reinforcement

More than half of AI users are reluctant to admit how much they rely on AI for important tasks and worry it makes them look replaceable, so voluntary self-report undercounts and must be paired with observation
Self-report overcounts because people exaggerate their AI use
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the finding that 52 percent of AI users are reluctant to admit using it for their most important tasks and 53 percent worry it makes them look replaceable. A baseline built only from voluntary self-report is therefore guaranteed to undercount, so you pair disclosure with observed evidence.

questions.question: McKinsey's survey found C-suite leaders estimated only 4 percent of employees use gen AI for at least 30 percent of their daily work, while 13 percent of employees reported doing so. Why does this perception gap matter for an adoption program?
options: It confirms that leadership's estimates are accurate enough to plan from
Because you cannot govern, measure, or scale AI use you do not know exists, so a baseline built on leadership belief rather than ground truth will mis-set every downstream goal
It only matters for marketing purposes and has no effect on goals or budget
It shows the program should focus on the sanctioned pilot and ignore everything else
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the whole point of the audit is to replace leadership belief with ground truth. A baseline built on a guess will mis-set goals, budget, policy, and incident response, because you cannot govern or measure what you cannot see.

questions.question: Why does Lesson 3 argue that self-reported time savings are unreliable as evidence that AI is paying off?
options: People tend to overestimate how long their tasks take and how much faster a tool makes them, so a survey of enthusiasm measures a feeling rather than a result
GitHub's controlled experiment proved that time-saved claims are always false
Self-reports are only unreliable in technology companies, not in operations
The McKinsey survey showed that time saved is never reallocated to new work
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 cites GitHub's own productivity research and reasoning that individuals are poor judges of how long tasks take, so a survey where people say they feel faster measures a feeling, not a P&L line. It recommends measuring a defined task before and after, throughput over a fixed window, or sampled time use instead.

questions.question: Lesson 3 splits the four metrics into two kinds. Which pair are the outcome metrics, the ones that tell you whether the work produced more value?
options: Time saved and quality
Usage and churn
Time saved and usage
Quality and churn
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 defines time saved and quality as the outcome metrics, because they ask whether the work costs less or the output is better. Usage and churn are the activity metrics, because they only ask whether people are actually using the tool, which is necessary but not sufficient proof of value.

questions.question: A rollout's usage peaks in week one at 60 percent reach but drops below 30 percent by week six. How should the adoption owner read this curve, based on the lesson?
options: The rollout failed, and it should be relaunched with a bigger launch event
The dip is the normal effect of novelty wearing off, so the owner should look at depth and churn, not reach, to find where real momentum is forming
High reach at launch proves the tool was adopted, and the drop is unrelated to the program
Usage falling below 30 percent means the tool itself is not useful and should be replaced
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the novelty effect as early enthusiasm driven by the fact that the thing is new, not that it is useful. A spike in reach is not the signal. The owner should watch depth (same people returning) and churn after the novelty period passes, because usage that survives novelty is the only kind that compounds.

questions.question: Mateo wants to grow adoption past the novelty dip. Which action best reflects the lesson's guidance to build breadth through depth?
options: Launch an org-wide push so every department tries the tool at least once
Broaden the tool license to the largest department first, even though it has no ready-made AI workflow
Find the adjacent workflow for the people already using the tool deeply and expand the tool into that workflow with the same users first
Reward any team that mentions AI in a meeting with a public shoutout
questions.explanation: The lesson says the people already using AI for one part of their job are the cheapest place to get the next win, so expansion should start with the next adjacent workflow for existing users. Breadth through depth, not depth through breadth. This mirrors Mateo bringing the billing team in after the password-reset win, rather than chasing the marketing department with no ready-made workflow.

questions.question: Lucia sets a target of twelve core workflows with documented, reviewed improvements by the end of the quarter, out of roughly thirty. Why does the lesson judge this target realistic rather than a guess or a fantasy?
options: Because twelve is a round number that looks good on a slide
Because it exceeds the goal-setting finding that specific difficult targets outperform vague instructions
Because it is grounded in a measured baseline and the audit's finding that most staff already use AI informally in value-ready workflows that can be formalized
Because it represents all thirty core workflows, showing full ambition
questions.explanation: The lesson's realism method grounds the target in the baseline value plus existing informal behavior the audit found, rather than inventing adoption from scratch. Lucia's target converts a plausible slice of already-happening informal use, which is why it is ambitious and reachable. A fantasy names a number no one can reach; a guess ignores the baseline.

questions.question: According to the McKinsey survey cited in Lesson 2, where do cost benefits from AI use most commonly concentrate?
options: Uniformly across every business function in the enterprise
In software engineering, manufacturing, and IT
Mostly in marketing and sales, with little elsewhere
In no single function, because the survey found no cost benefits
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 reports that McKinsey's survey found cost benefits from AI concentrate in software engineering, manufacturing, and IT, all high-volume, predictable-input, cheap-to-verify work. Revenue increases are most often reported in marketing and sales, strategy and corporate finance, and product and service development.

questions.question: Lesson 2 argues that two organizations using identical AI tools get very different results. What does the survey identify as the strongest lever behind meaningful value?
options: Purchasing a more advanced or expensive model
Redesigning the workflow around the model rather than bolting the tool onto an unchanged process
Giving every employee unrestricted access to the tool
Spending more on training sessions before any rollout
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 cites the survey finding that AI high performers are nearly three times as likely to have fundamentally redesigned individual workflows, and that workflow redesign is one of the strongest contributors to meaningful business impact. Value is a property of the redesigned workflow, not of the model.

questions.question: Lesson 3 describes the Boston Consulting Group field experiment and warns about the quality trap. What is the core warning about measuring speed without measuring quality?
options: On tasks inside the AI's capability frontier, people produced higher quality results, but on tasks outside it they were less likely to reach the correct solution, so speed alone can just reach wrong answers faster
Quality always rises automatically whenever a team works faster
Speed and quality move together, so measuring one is enough
The experiment found no speed gain at all, so time saved is a myth
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 uses the jagged-frontier experiment to show that within the AI's competence people were faster and produced higher quality work, but outside it they finished faster yet were about 19 percent less likely to be correct. Measuring only speed therefore optimizes for getting to bad outcomes sooner, so speed and quality must be tracked together.

questions.question: Two invoice specialists quietly went back to typing invoices by hand. Which action did Lucia take that most directly removed the friction driving their fallback?
options: She published the time-saved numbers in the weekly all-hands to prove the new way works
She expanded the tool to the load-confirmation workflow so the same team used it for more of their day
She changed the tool's settings so the confirmation prompt only appears when the tool's confidence is low, instead of on every invoice
She updated the standard operating procedure to make the AI-assisted workflow the documented default
questions.explanation: When Lucia asked the two specialists what pushed them back, they said the tool asked for a confirmation on every invoice and it felt like a nag. She removed that friction by making the confirmation appear only at low confidence. The other options are the short-term win, consolidation, and anchoring steps, which are real but not the friction fix.

questions.question: A stakeholder proposes 'share of employees who used AI this month' as the program's north-star metric. Why does this make a poor north-star, per the lesson?
options: It is too hard to measure reliably, so leadership will not trust it
It is a vanity metric that describes activity without describing value, so it can climb while the organization is no better off
It is a lagging indicator that only reports what already happened last month
It is not financially material enough to justify a budget request
questions.explanation: The lesson classifies the share of people using AI as a vanity metric, along with prompt counts and active-user counts. Such a metric scores activity, not value, and can rise while no real work improves. You may track it, but it should not be the north-star seat.

questions.question: Why does the lesson insist you pair the north-star metric with a guardrail metric rather than tracking only the north-star?
options: Because without a second number you cannot calculate a percentage
Because the north-star metric is unreliable and needs a backup for accuracy
Because a single metric can be met by harming quality, and the guardrail catches the cheap way when the measured improvement is not real
Because stakeholders always want to see more than one chart
questions.explanation: The lesson grounds the guardrail in Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure, because people chase the number the cheap way. A guardrail metric, such as the reviewer-correction rate, is the early warning that the north-star is being met by cutting quality.
